newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 12.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 12.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- ROW OVER UK CHALLENGE ON HOURS

Professor John Harrington has attacked the British government over its use of a report he compiled in its legal challenge to the EU 48-hour working week directive. He noted that contrary to UK government claims, long working hours are in fact a health issue. The British government is challenging the directive, passed under EU health and safety legislation and therefore binding. A European Court ruling is expected on Tuesday on the challenge. The UK wants the ruling overturned or passed under the social chapter, from which it has an opt-out, and is threatening the block agreement on a revised Maastricht treaty unless concessions are made.
-- BRITISH STEEL WARNS ON JOB CUTS

British Steel has warned that because of the increasing strength of the pound and intense foreign competition it may be forced to increase the rate at which it plans to shed staff in Britain. The warning came as the company announced a fall from 550 million stg to 262 million stg in pre-tax profits for the six months to the end of September. Over the period the company experienced extreme price volatility, with some forms of steel dropping in price by 45 per cent.
-- FLOTATION PLANNED FOR COLT TELECOMS

Colt Telecoms, the loss-making company offering business telecoms services within the City of London, is to float on the stock market within the next month. The shares will be pitched at investors in the UK and the US and is expected to see the company valued at around eight times current annual revenues. It is hoped that the offering will raise about 110 million dollars which will be used to help the company expand its existing network and perhaps to move into other European cities.
-- OXFORD ACTS TO SAVE BUSINESS SCHOOL PLAN

The ruling council at Oxford University is attempting to rescue plans for a 40 million sterling business school, which last week was rejected by academics at the college. The provision of funding for the project had been offered by leading Middle East businessman Wafic Said. There has been some controversy surrounding the use of a greenfield site at the college for the project, as the university on being given the site had promised there would be no development.
-- DEUTSCHE TELEKOM SHARE OFFER INCREASED BY 20 PER CENT

As a result of massive oversubscription Deutsche Telekom has decided to increase the number of shares being offered to investors in the company from 500 million to 600 million. The IPO, the largest in Europe, has received five times more applications for shares than are available. It is believed that the shares will be offered towards the upper value ceiling of DM30 per share, a move that will not prove popular with all analysts.
-- MONKS PROPOSES PACT WITH CBI

John Monks, the first head of the Trades Union Congress to be invited to address the annual meeting of the Confederation of British Industry, has suggested that steps be taken to improve levels of cooperation between employers and unions. Monks proposed a number of principles on which a common approach could be adopted by both camps on a range of issues, regardless of which party founded the next government. At the conference senior members of both the Conservatives and Labour took the opportunity to attack the other's policies on Europe, with the Tories warning of the adverse impact on business of Labour support for the social chapter.
-- GERMANY THREATENS TO STALL SINGLE CURRENCY AGREEMENT

A meeting of EU finance ministers in Brussels has seen Germany threaten to delay agreement being reached on the introduction of the single currency until rigid stability pact rules are set in place to deal with member states operating large budget deficits. Germany, along with the Netherlands, insist such rules are essential to maintain fiscal discipline among member states taking part in the euro. The rest of the EU sees the rules being suggested as too rigid. Kenneth Clarke for the UK insisted that states should be allowed occasional 'blips' in budget deficit levels without incurring heavy penalties.
-- UK AND ITALY JOIN EUROPEAN ARMS AGENCY

On Tuesday, both Italy and Britain will sign up to a new German-based agency which will set about fostering higher levels of cooperation between Europe's arms industries. At present France and Germany are the sole members of the alliance, which will seek to improve efficiencies in the field of defence procurement among member states. The body should reduce levels of duplication of work within the sector and apply common standards, improving the competitiveness of the sector.
-- BANKS SEEK DETAIL OF EUROTUNNEL SHARE ISSUE PROBE

A number of financial institutions based in London are seeking clarification on an investigation being launched by the Serious Fraud Office into alleged manipulation of the market for shares in Eurotunnel. The inquiry is being carried out on behalf of the French authorities amid claims regarding share sales in the company around the time of a rights issue in 1994. At the time there was an increase in the level of short-selling of shares in the company.
-- PLASTIC BANKNOTES MAY BE CONSIDERED FOR EURO

The Reserve Bank of Australia along with a UK polymers company are attempting to sell technology for the printing of the planned single currency that would result in euro banknotes being made of plastic. The joint venture formed by the two, Securency, has been involved in discussions on such a project with the European Monetary Institute. The use of plastic reduces the costs involved as notes last an average four times longer than traditional paper. BMC +44-171-377-1742
